questions.question_text: What is the architectural difference between git merge and git rebase? When should you use each?
questions.explanation: Git merge creates a non-destructive merge commit preserving exact history, while git rebase rewrites commit history by replaying commits on top of another branch for a linear log.
questions.reference_answer: Git merge creates a non-destructive merge commit preserving exact history, while git rebase rewrites commit history by replaying commits on top of another branch for a linear log.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Comparison of merge commit preservation vs linear history replaying.

questions.question_text: Explain how git cherry-pick works and provide a real-world scenario where it is necessary.
questions.explanation: Cherry-picking applies the changes introduced by an existing commit onto a different branch, commonly used to backport bug fixes from a development branch to a production release branch.
questions.reference_answer: Cherry-picking applies the changes introduced by an existing commit onto a different branch, commonly used to backport bug fixes from a development branch to a production release branch.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Definition of applying a specific commit hash to the current HEAD and a hotfix use case.

questions.question_text: What is the precise difference between git reset --soft, git reset --mixed, and git reset --hard?
questions.explanation: --soft moves HEAD only; --mixed (default) updates HEAD and clears the staging area; --hard updates HEAD, staging area, and working directory, discarding all uncommitted changes.
questions.reference_answer: --soft moves HEAD only; --mixed (default) updates HEAD and clears the staging area; --hard updates HEAD, staging area, and working directory, discarding all uncommitted changes.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Detailed breakdown of pointer movement and impact on staging area and working directory.

questions.question_text: How do you recover a commit or branch that was accidentally deleted or lost using git reflog?
questions.explanation: Git reflog records all movements of HEAD, allowing developers to locate the SHA hash of a lost commit or branch state prior to garbage collection and checkout a new branch from it.
questions.reference_answer: Git reflog records all movements of HEAD, allowing developers to locate the SHA hash of a lost commit or branch state prior to garbage collection and checkout a new branch from it.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Step-by-step commands using git reflog and git checkout/reset to restore dangling commits.

questions.question_text: What is a 'detached HEAD' state in Git, and how do you safely return to working on a branch?
questions.explanation: A detached HEAD occurs when checking out a specific commit instead of a branch. To save work done here, create a new branch using 'git checkout -b <branch-name>' before switching back.
questions.reference_answer: A detached HEAD occurs when checking out a specific commit instead of a branch. To save work done here, create a new branch using 'git checkout -b <branch-name>' before switching back.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Explanation of HEAD pointing directly to a commit hash instead of a branch ref.

questions.question_text: Explain the difference between git fetch, git pull, and git pull --rebase.
questions.explanation: Git fetch downloads remote updates without altering local branches. Git pull fetches and automatically merges, whereas git pull --rebase fetches and rebases local commits on top of remote changes.
questions.reference_answer: Git fetch downloads remote updates without altering local branches. Git pull fetches and automatically merges, whereas git pull --rebase fetches and rebases local commits on top of remote changes.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Distinction between downloading remote refs, downloading plus merging, and downloading plus rebasing.

questions.question_text: How do you squash multiple commits into a single clean commit before merging a pull request?
questions.explanation: Interactive rebase allows developers to combine ('squash' or 'fixup') multiple messy work-in-progress commits into a single cohesive commit with a clean descriptive message.
questions.reference_answer: Interactive rebase allows developers to combine ('squash' or 'fixup') multiple messy work-in-progress commits into a single cohesive commit with a clean descriptive message.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Interactive rebase workflow description using git rebase -i HEAD~n.

questions.question_text: What are Git hooks? Give examples of client-side vs. server-side hooks and their typical use cases.
questions.explanation: Git hooks are custom scripts triggered by core Git events. Client-side hooks (pre-commit) enforce linting/formatting; server-side hooks (pre-receive) enforce branch protection rules and security scanning.
questions.reference_answer: Git hooks are custom scripts triggered by core Git events. Client-side hooks (pre-commit) enforce linting/formatting; server-side hooks (pre-receive) enforce branch protection rules and security scanning.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Categorized examples of pre-commit, pre-push, and pre-receive scripts for linting and policy enforcement.

questions.question_text: How does Git detect and handle merge conflicts, and what is your step-by-step process for resolving them?
questions.explanation: Conflicts occur when concurrent changes modify identical lines in a file. Git injects conflict markers; developers inspect diffs, choose desired code blocks, stage files, and complete the merge.
questions.reference_answer: Conflicts occur when concurrent changes modify identical lines in a file. Git injects conflict markers; developers inspect diffs, choose desired code blocks, stage files, and complete the merge.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Conflict marker breakdown (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) and manual resolution workflow.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of .gitignore, and why might a file that is listed in .gitignore still be tracked by Git?
questions.explanation: .gitignore prevents untracked files from being staged. Files already tracked in Git history before being added to .gitignore remain tracked until explicitly untracked.
questions.reference_answer: .gitignore prevents untracked files from being staged. Files already tracked in Git history before being added to .gitignore remain tracked until explicitly untracked.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Explanation of exclusion patterns and cached tracked files needing git rm --cached.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between Git submodules and Git subtrees? When would you choose one over the other?
questions.explanation: Submodules reference a specific commit in an external repository URL (requiring explicit init/update), while subtrees merge external repository contents directly into a subdirectory of the main repo.
questions.reference_answer: Submodules reference a specific commit in an external repository URL (requiring explicit init/update), while subtrees merge external repository contents directly into a subdirectory of the main repo.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Comparison of pointer references (submodules) vs embedded subtree code integration.

questions.question_text: How do you temporarily stash uncommitted work, switch branches, and reapply the stash with conflict resolution?
questions.explanation: Git stash saves modified tracked files to a stack. Switching branches allows clean work; git stash pop re-applies changes, prompting manual resolution if conflicts arise with the new branch.
questions.reference_answer: Git stash saves modified tracked files to a stack. Switching branches allows clean work; git stash pop re-applies changes, prompting manual resolution if conflicts arise with the new branch.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Usage of git stash push, git checkout, git stash pop/apply, and conflict resolution.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between git revert and git reset in terms of shared collaboration history?
questions.explanation: Git reset rewrites history by moving the branch pointer backward (dangerous on shared remote branches). Git revert creates a new commit that undoes previous changes safely without rewriting history.
questions.reference_answer: Git reset rewrites history by moving the branch pointer backward (dangerous on shared remote branches). Git revert creates a new commit that undoes previous changes safely without rewriting history.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Safety analysis of rewriting public history (reset) vs creating compensatory inverse commits (revert).

questions.question_text: How do you permanently remove a sensitive file (like an API key or password) from your entire Git history using git filter-repo?
questions.explanation: Tools like git filter-repo rewrite all historical commits to purge sensitive files from object storage, requiring a force push and collaborator repository re-clones.
questions.reference_answer: Tools like git filter-repo rewrite all historical commits to purge sensitive files from object storage, requiring a force push and collaborator repository re-clones.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Command syntax and explanation of rewriting historical object trees and force-pushing.

questions.question_text: How do you manage multiple remote repositories and configure upstream tracking branches?
questions.explanation: Developers configure multiple remotes (e.g., origin for fork, upstream for main project) and link local branches to specific remote tracking branches using upstream configurations.
questions.reference_answer: Developers configure multiple remotes (e.g., origin for fork, upstream for main project) and link local branches to specific remote tracking branches using upstream configurations.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Syntax for git remote add, git fetch <remote>, and git branch --set-upstream-to.

questions.question_text: Define Continuous Integration (CI), Continuous Delivery (CD), and Continuous Deployment. What distinguishes Delivery from Deployment?
questions.explanation: CI automates code building and testing on every commit. Continuous Delivery ensures code is always release-ready with a manual promotion gate, whereas Continuous Deployment pushes every passing build automatically to production.
questions.reference_answer: CI automates code building and testing on every commit. Continuous Delivery ensures code is always release-ready with a manual promotion gate, whereas Continuous Deployment pushes every passing build automatically to production.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Clear lifecycle definitions emphasizing manual approval gates in Delivery vs fully automated production deployment.

questions.question_text: What are the key architectural components of a modern CI/CD pipeline (e.g., triggers, runners, steps, artifacts, deployment targets)?
questions.explanation: Pipelines comprise webhook event triggers, execution runners/agents, sequential job steps, intermediate build artifacts, and downstream environments (staging/production).
questions.reference_answer: Pipelines comprise webhook event triggers, execution runners/agents, sequential job steps, intermediate build artifacts, and downstream environments (staging/production).
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Comprehensive architectural workflow explanation from webhook trigger to target execution environment.

questions.question_text: How do you securely manage secrets, API tokens, and credentials in CI/CD pipelines (e.g., GitHub Actions, GitLab CI)?
questions.explanation: Secrets should be stored in encrypted platform secret stores or dynamic vaults (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) using OIDC token exchange rather than plain-text environment variables.
questions.reference_answer: Secrets should be stored in encrypted platform secret stores or dynamic vaults (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) using OIDC token exchange rather than plain-text environment variables.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Best practices including encrypted environment secrets, OIDC workload identity federation, and secret masking.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between pipeline caching and artifact storage, and how do they optimize build speed?
questions.explanation: Caching stores reusable dependency directories across pipeline runs to skip redundant downloads. Artifacts store built binaries or packages passed between sequential pipeline jobs.
questions.reference_answer: Caching stores reusable dependency directories across pipeline runs to skip redundant downloads. Artifacts store built binaries or packages passed between sequential pipeline jobs.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Distinction between dependency caches (node_modules) and immutable release build artifacts.

questions.question_text: Compare Blue-Green deployments and Canary deployments. What are the risks and benefits of each?
questions.explanation: Blue-Green maintains two identical production environments for instant cutover and instant rollback. Canary routes a small percentage of live user traffic to a new version to validate behavior under real load.
questions.reference_answer: Blue-Green maintains two identical production environments for instant cutover and instant rollback. Canary routes a small percentage of live user traffic to a new version to validate behavior under real load.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Risk-reward analysis comparing instant full-environment switching (Blue-Green) vs gradual subset traffic shifting (Canary).

questions.question_text: How do you implement automated quality gates (unit tests, integration tests, static code analysis, and security scanning) in a pipeline?
questions.explanation: Quality gates fail the pipeline automatically if code coverage drops, static analyzers detect critical bugs, or dependency scanners identify high-severity CVEs.
questions.reference_answer: Quality gates fail the pipeline automatically if code coverage drops, static analyzers detect critical bugs, or dependency scanners identify high-severity CVEs.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Pipeline stage sequencing enforcing test coverage thresholds, SonarQube analysis, and vulnerability checks.

questions.question_text: What is GitOps, and how does it differ from traditional push-based CI/CD pipelines?
questions.explanation: Traditional CI/CD pushes deployments from external build servers. GitOps uses an in-cluster operator to poll Git repositories and automatically reconcile live cluster state with declared desired state.
questions.reference_answer: Traditional CI/CD pushes deployments from external build servers. GitOps uses an in-cluster operator to poll Git repositories and automatically reconcile live cluster state with declared desired state.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Explanation of pull-based declarative reconciliation loops (ArgoCD/Flux) using Git as the single source of truth.

questions.question_text: How do you execute zero-downtime database migrations in a continuous delivery pipeline?
questions.explanation: Zero-downtime migrations use multi-step phases: Expand schema (add new nullable columns), deploy code compatible with old and new schemas, migrate data, and Contract schema (remove old columns).
questions.reference_answer: Zero-downtime migrations use multi-step phases: Expand schema (add new nullable columns), deploy code compatible with old and new schemas, migrate data, and Contract schema (remove old columns).
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Expand-and-contract (backward-compatible) schema migration strategy description.

questions.question_text: What is a self-hosted runner/agent, and when should an organization use one instead of cloud-managed runners?
questions.explanation: Self-hosted runners run on private infrastructure, enabling access to internal VPC resources, custom hardware (GPUs), specialized compliance tooling, or reduction of cloud build minute costs.
questions.reference_answer: Self-hosted runners run on private infrastructure, enabling access to internal VPC resources, custom hardware (GPUs), specialized compliance tooling, or reduction of cloud build minute costs.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Use cases covering private network access, specialized hardware, cost control, and data residency.

questions.question_text: Explain matrix builds in pipeline configurations. Give a practical scenario where a matrix build is essential.
questions.explanation: Matrix builds dynamically expand a single job template into multiple concurrent jobs across variable parameters, essential for testing Python packages across multiple OS and Python versions.
questions.reference_answer: Matrix builds dynamically expand a single job template into multiple concurrent jobs across variable parameters, essential for testing Python packages across multiple OS and Python versions.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Definition of parallel job generation across multiple OS, runtime, and architecture permutations.

questions.question_text: What is your automated rollback strategy when a production deployment fails health checks?
questions.explanation: Pipelines monitor post-deployment health metrics and error rates; if thresholds are breached, the orchestration platform automatically shifts traffic back to the stable replica set or previous container tag.
questions.reference_answer: Pipelines monitor post-deployment health metrics and error rates; if thresholds are breached, the orchestration platform automatically shifts traffic back to the stable replica set or previous container tag.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Automated rollback workflow utilizing load balancer health checks, canary error thresholds, or previous image rollback.

questions.question_text: How do you perform infrastructure testing (e.g., Terratest) as part of your CI workflow?
questions.explanation: Terratest allows writing automated tests in Go that provision real cloud resources using Terraform, validate assertions, and guarantee cleanup even if tests fail.
questions.reference_answer: Terratest allows writing automated tests in Go that provision real cloud resources using Terraform, validate assertions, and guarantee cleanup even if tests fail.

questions.question_text: What are feature flags (toggles) decouple software deployment from feature release?
questions.explanation: Feature flags wrap new code paths in conditional checks, allowing code to be merged and deployed safely to production while remaining hidden until business readiness.

questions.question_text: What is a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), and why is its generation critical in modern supply chain security?
questions.explanation: An SBOM is a formal inventory of all open-source libraries, packages, and dependencies included in a software build, essential for rapid CVE impact analysis during zero-day vulnerabilities.
questions.reference_answer: An SBOM is a formal inventory of all open-source libraries, packages, and dependencies included in a software build, essential for rapid CVE impact analysis during zero-day vulnerabilities.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Definition of structured component manifests (SPDX/CycloneDX) used for vulnerability tracking.

questions.question_text: How do you optimize pipeline execution time and resource consumption when working with large monorepos?
questions.explanation: Monorepo CI optimization involves path-based job filtering to build and test only packages affected by a given pull request commit diff.
questions.reference_answer: Monorepo CI optimization involves path-based job filtering to build and test only packages affected by a given pull request commit diff.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Techniques utilizing sparse checkouts, changed-file detection tools (Nx, Bazel), and selective job execution.

questions.question_text: Explain the fundamental differences between Virtual Machines (VMs) and Containers regarding architecture and OS resource sharing.
questions.explanation: VMs run full guest operating systems on top of a hypervisor, consuming high overhead. Containers share the host OS kernel via namespaces and cgroups, offering lightweight isolation.
questions.reference_answer: VMs run full guest operating systems on top of a hypervisor, consuming high overhead. Containers share the host OS kernel via namespaces and cgroups, offering lightweight isolation.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Contrast hypervisor virtualization of full guest OS instances with container user-space sharing of host kernel.

questions.question_text: How do Docker image layers work, and why are multi-stage builds critical for reducing image size and attack surface?
questions.explanation: Docker images consist of cached read-only filesystem layers. Multi-stage builds compile applications in heavy SDK images and copy only the final runtime binary into a lean production image, omitting build tools.
questions.reference_answer: Docker images consist of cached read-only filesystem layers. Multi-stage builds compile applications in heavy SDK images and copy only the final runtime binary into a lean production image, omitting build tools.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Explanation of UnionFS read-only layers and copying compiled binaries into minimal scratch/alpine runtime stages.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile? Can you combine them?
questions.explanation: ENTRYPOINT sets the default command executed at container startup. CMD provides default arguments to ENTRYPOINT, which can be overridden easily via command-line arguments during 'docker run'.
questions.reference_answer: ENTRYPOINT sets the default command executed at container startup. CMD provides default arguments to ENTRYPOINT, which can be overridden easily via command-line arguments during 'docker run'.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Explanation of ENTRYPOINT as fixed executable and CMD as default arguments that can be overridden.

questions.question_text: How do Docker volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs mounts differ in data persistence and performance?
questions.explanation: Volumes are managed entirely by Docker in host storage (best practice for persistence). Bind mounts map host filesystem paths directly into containers. Tmpfs mounts store ephemeral data directly in host memory.
questions.reference_answer: Volumes are managed entirely by Docker in host storage (best practice for persistence). Bind mounts map host filesystem paths directly into containers. Tmpfs mounts store ephemeral data directly in host memory.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Comparison of managed Docker storage (volumes), host directory mounting (bind mounts), and RAM storage (tmpfs).

questions.question_text: Explain Docker networking modes: Bridge, Host, Overlay, and None. When do you use each?
questions.explanation: Bridge is default for standalone containers. Host removes network isolation for maximum performance. Overlay enables secure multi-host container communication across Docker Swarm or Kubernetes clusters.
questions.reference_answer: Bridge is default for standalone containers. Host removes network isolation for maximum performance. Overlay enables secure multi-host container communication across Docker Swarm or Kubernetes clusters.
questions.grading_rubric: Award 5 marks when the answer covers: Use case overview for standalone private networks (bridge), host network sharing (host), multi-host swarm networking (overlay), and isolated containers (none).

questions.question_text: How do you write a secure Dockerfile (e.g., running as a non-root user, pinning base images, scanning for vulnerabilities)?
questions.explanation: Secure Dockerfiles avoid running as root by creating a dedicated user, pin base images with specific SHA256 digests rather than 'latest', and integrate vulnerability scanning tools.
questions.reference_answer: Secure Dockerfiles avoid running as root by creating a dedicated user, pin base images with specific SHA256 digests rather than 'latest', and integrate vulnerability scanning tools.

questions.question_text: What causes container disk bloat, and how do you clean up unused images, volumes, and build caches (docker system prune)?
questions.explanation: Unused container disk bloat accumulates from dangling image layers, stopped containers, and unused build caches. 'docker system prune' safely reclaims this storage space.

questions.explanation: HEALTHCHECK instructions run commands inside containers periodically. Orchestrators monitor these health states to restart unhealthy containers or stop routing traffic to them.

questions.question_text: What is Docker Compose, and how do you handle service dependencies, health checks, and scaling locally?
questions.explanation: Docker Compose defines multi-container applications in a single YAML file, coordinating service startup ordering, health conditions, and local development environments.

questions.question_text: How do you debug a crashing or unresponsive container using docker logs, docker exec, and container introspection?
questions.explanation: Developers inspect container failure causes by checking stdout logs with 'docker logs', executing interactive shell commands via 'docker exec -it', and inspecting container metadata with 'docker inspect'.

questions.question_text: How do Linux namespaces and cgroups power container isolation and resource limitation?
questions.explanation: Namespaces virtualize system resources (PID, NET, MNT) so processes see an isolated environment. Control groups (cgroups) restrict resource usage (CPU, memory, I/O) allocated to container processes.
questions.reference_answer: Namespaces virtualize system resources (PID, NET, MNT) so processes see an isolated environment. Control groups (cgroups) restrict resource usage (CPU, memory, I/O) allocated to container processes.

questions.question_text: How do you share local Unix sockets or files securely between a host machine and a running container?
questions.explanation: Host sockets and files are shared by mounting specific host paths into container mount points using volume flags (e.g., -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock).

questions.question_text: What is a container registry (e.g., AWS ECR, GitHub Packages), and how do image tags and immutable digests differ?
questions.explanation: Image tags can be overwritten in registries pointing to different builds. Immutable image digests (sha256:...) guarantee exact binary reproducibility and supply chain integrity.

questions.question_text: How do you handle graceful shutdowns (SIGTERM handling) in containerized applications to prevent dropped connections?
questions.explanation: When stopping, Docker sends SIGTERM. Applications must trap this signal, stop accepting new requests, finish processing in-flight requests, and exit cleanly before the forced SIGKILL timeout.

questions.explanation: Kube-apiserver exposes the Kubernetes API. Etcd stores cluster state reliably. Kube-scheduler assigns pods to worker nodes. Controller-manager runs background reconciliation loops.

questions.explanation: ConfigMaps store non-confidential configuration data. Secrets store sensitive data (base64 encoded). Both can be injected into pods as environment variables or mounted files.

questions.explanation: Requests reserve minimum compute resources for scheduling. Limits cap maximum resource consumption. If a container exceeds its memory limit, the Linux kernel terminates the process with an OOMKilled exit code.

questions.explanation: Startup probes verify slow-starting app initialization. Readiness probes control when traffic is routed to pods. Liveness probes restart dead or deadlocked containers automatically.

questions.question_text: How do Persistent Volumes (PV), Persistent Volume Claims (PVC), and StorageClasses work together?
